doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Why musicians accept the sacrifice
summary: Music is addictive and a labor of love; a culture without the arts has no soul.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: I guess you’d have to want to play awful bad.

Well music is like so many forms of art, it’s a labor of love. And the music business, you talk about being addictive, it’s as addictive as any narcotic man. I mean once you start playing, especially if you’re playing with guys that can play and you get a certain cohesiveness and a certain satisfaction. And then the people, the audience, you bring so much joy to them. Husband and wife, or girlfriend and boyfriend, or fiancees, they’ll come out and maybe that’s a very memorable night to them. Maybe you played their favorite song and well they’ll tell you what their song is and they go home with a pocketful of memories. And if you’re lucky enough to have a CD or a recording or tape or something, they can take it home with them. And it’s just — and without music and the arts, your culture has no soul, no soul. As a matter of fact you don’t have any culture you know. So there’s just a whole lot that goes with it, and so you just make the sacrifice.
